summary: This RFC defines a model of service for Internet multicasting and proposes an extension to IP for it. The RFC asks for discussion. It was replaced by RFC 988.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of sending the same letter to each person separately, you send it once to a group address and everyone in the group gets it.

questions: how do you join a multicast group
what is the difference between multicast and broadcast
subtitle: Sending a single packet to a group of hosts over the Internet.

tldr.problem: Internet applications need to send the same data to multiple hosts, but existing IP only supports sending to individual addresses or broadcast to everyone.
tldr.mechanism: The host group model extends IP to recognize special group addresses; any host can join a group, and a packet sent to a group address is delivered to all current members of that group.
tldr.outcome: Multicast delivery became a core Internet capability, enabling efficient group communication for applications like conferencing, replicated databases, and distributed computing. RFC 966 was replaced by RFC 988.

facts.label: Destination types
facts.value: Group addresses represent zero or more hosts

facts.label: Membership
facts.value: Hosts join and leave groups dynamically

facts.label: Sender requirement
facts.value: Sender need not be a member of the destination group

today: RFC 966 was superseded by RFC 988, which refined the multicast model. IP multicast, based on these core ideas, became standardized and is widely deployed in the modern Internet for video conferencing, streaming, and group applications. The basic concept of multicast addresses and group membership remains central to how multicast works today.

sections.title: The Need for Multicast
sections.content:
Applications often need to send data to multiple hosts at once. Before multicast, the only way to reach a group was for the sender to know each host's individual address and send duplicate packets to each one. This wastes bandwidth, gateway resources and sender effort. When the same packet travels the same network links multiple times, it prevents local networks from using their own multicast capabilities. For example, an Ethernet can deliver one packet to many machines at once, but without IP multicast the sender has to create separate copies for the network to forward.

Multicast has two main uses. First, it enables service discovery: a client sends one query to a well-known multicast address and all matching servers respond. Second, it supports applications like video conferencing and replicated databases that naturally need to send data to a set of cooperating hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: If everyone in a club needs to hear a message, it is faster to ring a bell everyone listens to than to tell each person one at a time.

sections.title: Host Groups as Addresses
sections.content:
The RFC extends IP's address space to include host group addresses in addition to individual host addresses. A host group is simply a set of zero or more Internet hosts. Unlike unicast (one sender to one receiver), a host does not need to be a member of a group to send to it. Hosts can join and leave groups dynamically, and a host may belong to multiple groups at once.

The RFC distinguishes between permanent groups (assigned by Internet administrators like well-known port numbers) and transient groups (created dynamically by applications as needed). A permanent group might be for all name servers or all boot servers; a transient group might exist only while a video conference is happening.
sections.plainLanguage: A group address is like the address of a club meeting room instead of a person's home. Anyone can send a letter to the room, and whoever is inside gets it.

sections.title: Creating and Managing Groups
sections.content:
The RFC defines three operations available to hosts. CreateGroup creates a new transient group and returns a unique group address; the requesting host becomes the first member. JoinGroup adds a host to an existing group (permanent or transient), optionally with an access key to control membership. LeaveGroup removes a host from a group. A transient group automatically ceases to exist when its last member leaves.

Transmission uses a Send operation that includes a distance parameter, allowing senders to limit how far their multicast packet travels. This enables expanding-ring search: try nearby servers first, then progressively widen the search. Reception is unchanged: hosts receive incoming multicast datagrams destined to any of their joined groups, alongside unicast packets.
sections.plainLanguage: You can start a group and invite people to join it. You can also limit how far your message travels, like saying 'only ask people in this building' before asking 'okay, now ask the whole city'.

sections.title: How the Internet Delivers Multicast Packets
sections.content:
Each gateway maintains three data structures: a routing table (standard IP routes), a network membership table (which networks contain members of each group), and a local host membership table (which local hosts are in each group). When a gateway receives a multicast packet, it looks up where members of the destination group are located. For each network that contains members, it either sends the packet directly on that network (using the network's local multicast address if supported) or forwards it to another gateway that connects to a member network.

The RFC acknowledges optimization challenges. On local-area networks that support multicast natively (like Ethernet), the mapping is direct. On networks without native multicast support, the gateway might broadcast to all hosts or maintain a list of specific hosts. The delivery mechanism must scale as the Internet grows, avoid systematic gaps in coverage, and not regularly send duplicate packets to the same host.
sections.plainLanguage: The network post office looks up which neighborhoods have people in the group, and sends copies to each neighborhood. If the neighborhood has a group mailbox, it delivers there; otherwise it tells each person individually.

sections.title: Control and Limits
sections.content:
The RFC identifies two design challenges. One is authentication and access control: gateways must decide which hosts can create groups and who can join restricted groups, based on the host's identity. The RFC notes this is a new problem for the Internet—individual addresses have always been administratively assigned, but multicast introduces dynamic binding that requires gatekeeping.

The RFC proposes two address classes for group addresses. One approach reserves a portion of the 32-bit IP space (perhaps using Class D addresses starting with binary 1110) for group identifiers, subdividing into permanent and transient ranges. A new IP option specifies administrative distance (how many administrative boundaries to cross), allowing organizations to limit multicast scope by organizational unit rather than just network hop count.
sections.plainLanguage: You need to know who is allowed to create a group and who is allowed to join a group. You also need a rule to say 'this message only goes to people in our building' or 'this message can go anywhere'.

sections.title: Comparison to Other Approaches
sections.content:
Several earlier proposals tried to solve the group-communication problem differently. Some suggested using broadcast, where packets go to everyone on a network or internetwork. But broadcast wastes resources on uninvolved hosts and does not scale. Others proposed allowing a single IP datagram to carry multiple destination addresses; the gateways would replicate and forward it. This avoids some inefficiency but does not let senders avoid knowing all recipient addresses, and it cannot exploit local network multicast capabilities.

The host group model differs by providing a true group abstraction: a single address representing a dynamic set of members, with the binding of address to members maintained by the network infrastructure. This allows service discovery and scales to large groups and large internetworks.
sections.plainLanguage: Some people said 'just send to everyone', but that wastes resources on people who do not care. Some said 'put all addresses in the packet', but then you have to know every person's address. Host groups let the network remember who is in the group.
